title: Certified Letters: Everything You Need to Know
summary: Learn how certified letters work, when to use them, and what documents require certified mail. Find out how to track, send, and secure delivery for important communications.
body_text: ❓What is a certified letter? A certified letter is a service offered by the United States Postal Service (USPS) that provides senders with proof of mailing and delivery. When you send a certified letter, you receive a mailing receipt and a unique tracking number. The recipient must sign for the letter upon delivery, and that signature can be returned to you if you request a return receipt. This way, you have clear evidence that the letter was delivered and received. Certified letters are commonly used when the contents are important or time-sensitive, such as legal documents, tax correspondence, or employment-related notices. By requiring a signature, the service helps prevent disputes about whether the recipient received the communication. It’s a reliable way to send critical information, especially when accountability matters. ❓How does certified mail work? Certified mail works by creating a paper trail that verifies every step of the mailing process. After preparing your letter and addressing the envelope, you visit your local post office and fill out PS Form 3800, which includes a barcode for tracking. You then attach the form to the envelope and pay the postage fee, along with an extra charge for the certified service. The USPS records the date and time your letter was mailed and provides tracking updates along the way. Once the letter arrives, the recipient must sign for it. If you request a return receipt (PS Form 3811), you’ll receive a copy of the recipient’s signature, either by mail or electronically. This end-to-end documentation makes certified mail especially useful for legal notices, compliance letters, and contract-related communication. ❓Why would someone send a certified letter? People send certified letters when they need documented proof that a piece of mail was sent, delivered, and received. This is particularly important in scenarios involving legal liability, contract enforcement, or compliance requirements. For example, you might use certified mail to send a notice of lease termination to a tenant, a final warning to an employee, or a payment dispute to a vendor. Government agencies also rely heavily on certified mail. The IRS, for instance, sends audit notices and deficiency letters through this method to ensure proper delivery and to establish a record in case of legal challenges. Similarly, lawyers, property managers, and HR professionals use certified letters to handle sensitive communications where it’s crucial to confirm delivery. In all these cases, certified mail protects the sender by providing a clear trail of accountability. ❓Who typically uses certified mail? Certified mail is used by both individuals and organizations that need verifiable delivery of important documents. Among the most frequent users are: Government agencies , like the IRS or Social Security Administration, which must prove they notified citizens properly. Law firms , which use certified letters to send summons, subpoenas, and notices. Employers , especially HR departments , that send termination notices, COBRA paperwork, or final paychecks. Landlords and tenants , for delivering formal notices such as rent increases or eviction letters. Businesses and consumers , who want to ensure delivery of disputes, invoices, or legally binding letters. In every case, the user values the peace of mind and legal documentation that certified mail provides. ❓What kinds of documents are usually sent via certified mail? Certified mail is typically used to send documents that carry legal or financial weight. These may include : Court documents like summonses, complaints, and eviction notices Tax correspondence from the IRS or state agencies Employment-related letters including terminations, benefits eligibility, and FMLA paperwork Contracts or contract-related communications such as breach notices or terminations Billing disputes or formal complaints Using certified mail for these types of documents ensures that there is a permanent, legally recognized record of communication. That’s particularly important when deadlines, regulations, or legal requirements are involved. 💡If you're sending important documents, you might also want to understand the meaning and uses of certified copies . ❓Can you send certified mail to a PO Box? Yes, you can send certified mail to a PO Box. When a certified letter arrives at a PO Box, the USPS does not place it directly in the box. Instead, a delivery notice is left inside the box, informing the recipient that a certified letter is waiting for them at the service counter. The recipient must go to the counter, present a valid ID, and sign for the letter in person. This approach preserves the integrity of the certified process. Even though the recipient isn’t receiving the letter directly in their box, the requirement to sign for it ensures that only the intended party can access the contents. This is especially important for legal and official mail, where proof of receipt matters. 💡 If you're sending an appeal regarding an important decision, our step-by-step guide on how to write an appeal letter might be helpful. ❓How long does it take for certified mail to be delivered? Certified mail is usually delivered within 1 to 3 business days when sent via First-Class Mail. If you use Priority Mail as the base service, the delivery may be even faster. However, delivery time can be affected by weekends, holidays, and destination distance. While USPS generally meets its timeframes, it’s always wise to plan for a 5 to 7-day window to allow for any unforeseen delays. What sets certified mail apart isn’t the speed but the accountability. You’ll be able to track the letter throughout its journey and confirm that it reached the right hands. For that reason, certified mail is ideal for documents that may not be urgent but still require verified delivery. ❓Does certified mail require a signature? Yes, certified mail always requires a signature from the recipient upon delivery. The USPS will not drop off the letter unless someone signs for it. If no one is available to sign, the carrier leaves a delivery notice and holds the letter at the local post office. The recipient can then retrieve it in person by signing for it at the counter. For added control, senders can request a return receipt, which provides a copy of the recipient’s signature. They can also use options like restricted delivery or an adult signature required to ensure that only a specific person, or someone 21 or older, can sign for the mail. This signature process is what makes certified mail legally valid as evidence of delivery. ❓Are there any extra security options when sending a certified letter? Yes, USPS offers several add-ons that enhance the security of certified mail: Return Receipt : Provides proof of delivery with the recipient's signature, either in physical or electronic format. Restricted Delivery : Limits who can sign for the letter, typically only the person addressed. Adult Signature Required : Ensures only someone age 21 or older can receive the letter. Adult Signature Restricted Delivery : Combines both restrictions, requiring the named adult recipient to be the one who signs. These options are particularly useful for sensitive communications involving legal matters, financial data, or personal privacy. They allow the sender to tightly control who can receive the mail and to document every step of the process for future reference. See what else we're writing about on the ROGER Blog.

title: Hiring Your First Employee in India? Do Not Skip This One Step
summary: Protect your small business by verifying your first employee. Learn why digital identity verification is a fast, affordable, and crucial step for founders.
body_text: Insights & Resources Hiring Your First Employee in India? Do Not Skip This One Step July 30, 2026 Shashank Yadav No comments yet There is a moment every Indian founder and small business owner remembers. The moment you realize you cannot do everything alone anymore. The orders are piling up, the phone will not stop ringing, and you are working 16 hour days just to keep things moving. You need help. You need your first hire. It is exciting. It is also terrifying. Because this one person is going to shape the culture of your business, handle your money, interact with your customers, and represent your brand when you are not around. Getting this hire right matters more than almost any other decision you will make in the early days. Most founders obsess over the right things. They think about skills, salary, culture fit, availability. They write job descriptions, conduct interviews, call references. But there is one step that the vast majority of first time employers in India skip entirely. Identity verification. Not because they do not care. But because they do not know how fast and affordable it has become. And because they assume it is something only big companies need to do. That assumption can cost you everything you have built. Why Your First Hire Carries More Risk Than Any Other In a large company, a bad hire is a problem. In a company of one becoming a company of two, a bad hire is a catastrophe. Think about what your first employee will have access to. They will likely know your bank details, your supplier relationships, your customer list, and your daily revenue. They will have keys to your shop, access to your inventory, and the password to your billing software. In many cases, they will be alone in the store or office when you step out. You are not just hiring an employee. You are handing a stranger the keys to your livelihood. Now consider this. Studies show that 30 to 35 percent of resumes in India contain some form of misrepresentation. That number includes candidates who inflate job titles, fabricate work experience, and in some cases use borrowed or fake identity documents. The candidate sitting across from you might be perfectly honest. Or they might be one of the three in ten who are not. When you are a 500 person company, those odds are manageable. You have systems, oversight, and redundancy. When you are a one person company making your first hire, those odds are a coin flip on your entire business. What Identity Verification Actually Means (It Is Simpler Than You Think) When most first time employers hear “identity verification” or “background check,” they picture a corporate process with thick files, weeks of waiting, and a bill that would eat into next month’s rent. That picture is outdated. Digital identity verification in 2026 means entering a candidate’s PAN number, Voter ID number, Driving Licence number, and UAN into a platform that checks each one against the actual government database. The Income Tax Department confirms whether the PAN is real and who it belongs to. The Election Commission confirms the Voter ID. The Transport Department confirms the Driving Licence status. EPFO confirms the UAN and shows which employers actually paid PF contributions for this person. The whole process takes about ten minutes. It costs under Rs 500 for all four checks. And it gives you something that no interview, no reference call, and no gut feeling can provide. Independent, government verified confirmation that this person is who they say they are. You do not need an HR department. You do not need a BGV agency. You do not need a subscription or a contract. You just need ten minutes and a platform like ID Verify by SalaryBox. The Five Things Verification Tells You Before You Hand Over the Keys Let me walk you through exactly what you learn from each check and why it matters when you are making your very first hire. Your candidate’s real name This sounds basic, but it is not. When you run a PAN check, the Income Tax Department returns the full legal name linked to that PAN number. If the candidate told you their name is Amit Sharma but the PAN comes back registered to Vikas Gupta, you have just caught something that no interview would have revealed. The person may be using a relative’s PAN, a stolen document, or a completely fabricated identity. For a first time employer, this is the most important piece of information you can get. If you do not know someone’s real name, you do not know who is in your shop. Whether their Driving Licence is actually valid If your first hire involves any driving at all, this check is critical. Maybe you are hiring a delivery person, or a store assistant who will sometimes run errands in the company vehicle. A DL check tells you whether the licence is active, expired, suspended, or cancelled. It tells you which vehicle types the person is authorized to drive. And it tells you about any past suspensions. A candidate can hand you a perfectly genuine looking Driving Licence that was suspended last month for reckless driving. You would never know from looking at the card. The Transport Department database tells you in seconds. Where they actually worked before This is where UAN verification becomes incredibly powerful for first time employers. When someone tells you they spent two years working at a well known retail chain, you want to believe them. But you have no way to verify that claim by looking at an experience letter, because experience letters can be printed on any letterhead. UAN verification goes straight to the EPFO database and shows you which companies actually contributed PF for this person, with dates of joining and leaving. If they claimed two years at a retail chain and the UAN shows no PF contributions from that company, you have your answer. The experience was fabricated. For a first time employer who has never done a reference check and may not even know how, UAN verification does the heavy lifting automatically. Whether their identity is consistent across documents This is the part that makes digital verification truly powerful. When you run all four checks together, the platform compares the results. Does the name on the PAN match the name on the Voter ID? Does the date of birth on the DL match the UAN record? Do the addresses make sense together? Consistent details across multiple government databases give you high confidence that the person is genuine. Conflicts between databases are a flashing warning sign. ID Verify by SalaryBox does this cross record comparison automatically and highlights any mismatches so you do not need to manually compare four sets of results. A documented record that you did your homework This might not feel important on day one, but it matters enormously down the road. Every verification generates a downloadable PDF report with timestamped results. This report goes into your employee’s file and serves as proof that you exercised due diligence. If anything goes wrong later, whether it is theft, fraud, a legal dispute, or an insurance claim, this report demonstrates that you verified the employee’s identity before hiring them. Without it, you are exposed to negligent hiring arguments, insurance claim denials, and regulatory questions under the DPDP Act 2023. The Mistakes First Time Employers Make Having seen how thousands of Indian small businesses handle their first few hires, certain patterns come up again and again. The most common mistake is hiring based entirely on a personal impression from the interview. First time employers often trust their instincts because they have to make decisions quickly and do not have a structured process. But interviews measure communication skills and likability, not honesty. Only 19 percent of hiring managers say they can reliably spot a dishonest candidate in an interview. That number is likely even lower for founders who have never hired before. The second mistake is accepting photocopied documents at face value. A candidate hands over a photocopy of their PAN card, Aadhaar, and maybe an experience letter. The employer files these away feeling like they have done their due diligence. But a photocopy tells you nothing about whether the document is genuine, active, or belongs to the person who handed it to you. High quality fake PAN cards cost less than Rs 500 on the black market. Visual inspection is not verification. The third mistake is rushing because you are desperate for help. Your business is growing, you are overwhelmed, and you need someone yesterday. So you skip the checks, fast track the onboarding, and hope for the best. This is the most expensive shortcut in business. The cost of waiting two more days to verify a candidate is zero. The cost of hiring the wrong person can run into lakhs. The fourth mistake is assuming that verification is only for big companies. This might be the most harmful misconception of all. Big companies have legal teams, insurance policies, and redundancy built into their operations. A bad hire hurts them, but it does not destroy them. A small business owner making their first hire has none of those safety nets. If anything, they need verification more than anyone. Your First Hire Checklist (With Verification Built In) Here is a practical step by step checklist for making your first hire in India, with identity verification built into the process where it belongs. Before you start looking, get your business basics in order. Register with the state labour department if required. Set up a PF account if you expect to have more than 20 employees (or voluntarily for fewer). Open a separate bank account for salary payments. Draft a simple offer letter template. During the search, write a clear job description. Use personal networks, job platforms, or local postings. Screen resumes or applications for relevant experience. During the interview, assess skills, attitude, and cultural fit. Ask specific questions about their previous roles. Collect their PAN number, Voter ID number, DL number (if relevant), and UAN (if they claim prior employment). Before the offer, run identity verification through ID Verify by SalaryBox. Review the cross record analysis. If everything checks out, proceed. If there are discrepancies, investigate before committing. Download the verification report and save it. After the offer, share a written offer letter that includes a clause stating employment is contingent on successful verification. Complete onboarding paperwork. Set clear expectations for the first 30, 60, and 90 days. This checklist adds about ten minutes and under Rs 500 to your hiring process. It could save you from a disaster that derails your entire business. What Happens When First Time Employers Skip Verification The stories are depressingly predictable because the pattern is always the same. A first time employer in Nagpur opened a small electronics repair shop and hired a technician based on a friend’s recommendation. No verification was done. The technician had access to customer devices, including phones and laptops brought in for repair. Within two months, three customers reported data theft from their devices. The technician had been copying contacts and personal photos. When the shop owner tried to file a police complaint, he realized the address on the technician’s submitted documents was fake. The person could not be traced. A young entrepreneur in Bangalore launched a cloud kitchen and hired a cook through a walk in interview. The cook claimed four years of experience at two restaurants. No verification was done. The cook had basic skills but had fabricated his experience, and his actual employment, confirmed later through a belated UAN check, showed he had worked only at a small dhaba for six months before being let go. The kitchen’s food quality suffered, customer complaints mounted, and the entrepreneur spent Rs 2 lakh in the first three months on wasted ingredients, bad reviews, and eventually rehiring. A freelance graphic designer in Mumbai grew her business to the point where she needed an assistant to handle client communication and invoicing. She hired a young woman who seemed organized and professional. No identity verification was done. Three months later, the assistant began diverting small client payments to her own account. When confronted, she quit immediately. The designer discovered that the PAN card on file belonged to someone else entirely. Recovery was impossible. Each of these situations would have been prevented by a ten minute identity check. How ID Verify by SalaryBox Is Built for First Time Employers ID Verify was not designed for enterprise HR departments with dedicated compliance teams. It was designed for people like you. Business owners making their first hire, their fifth hire, or their fifteenth. People who need fast, clear, affordable answers about whether a candidate is who they claim to be. There is no setup process. You visit verify.salarybox.in, create an account, and run your first check in the same sitting. There is no demo to schedule, no salesperson to speak with, no contract to sign. You run PAN, Voter ID, Driving Licence, and UAN checks in a single flow. The platform handles the government database queries, the cross record analysis, and the report generation. You review the results and make your decision. You pay only for the checks you run. If you hire one person this year, you pay for one set of checks. There is no subscription, no annual commitment, and no minimum volume. The PDF report you download becomes the first document in your new employee’s file. It is your proof of due diligence, your compliance record, and your insurance against things going wrong. Your first hire shapes everything that comes after. Make sure you know who you are hiring. Start your first verification at verify.salarybox.in Frequently Asked Questions I am hiring my first employee ever. Is verification really necessary at this stage? It is most necessary at this stage. Your first employee will have more access, more responsibility, and more influence on your business than any subsequent hire. They are also the hire you have the least experience evaluating. Verification costs under Rs 500 and takes ten minutes. There is no rational reason to skip it, and the downside of skipping it can be catastrophic. My first hire is a family friend. Should I still verify? Yes. Verification is a business process, not a personal judgement. Running a quick identity check on a family friend is not an insult. It is a professional standard that protects both of you. If their documents check out, which they almost certainly will, you have peace of mind and a compliance record. If something unexpected surfaces, you have avoided a problem before it started. I do not have a PF account yet. Can I still verify employees? Yes. Verifying an employee’s identity does not require you to have your own PF registration. You are checking their documents against government databases. Their PAN check goes to the Income Tax Department, their Voter ID to the Election Commission, and so on. Your own PF status is irrelevant to the verification process. What if my first hire is a fresher with no work history? Freshers will not have a UAN because they have never been in formal employment with PF contributions. That is completely normal. Run PAN and Voter ID checks to confirm their identity. These two checks together provide strong two source verification. The absence of a UAN is only a concern if the candidate claims previous experience that should have generated PF contributions. How do I explain to the candidate that I want to verify their documents? Keep it simple and professional. Tell the candidate that identity verification is a standard part of your hiring process for all roles. Most candidates expect this and cooperate without any hesitation. The small number who resist usually have a reason for resisting, and that resistance is itself informative. What legal requirements should I know about before verifying? Under the DPDP Act 2023, you need the candidate’s written consent before processing their personal data for verification. Use a simple consent form that explains which checks will be run. Store the consent form along with the verification report. That is the extent of the legal requirement for the verification itself. Related Shashank Yadav Leave a Reply Cancel reply

title: What's the Best Way to Build Scorecards for Ramping SDRs?
summary: Find out how Ambition lets you tailor goals for new reps without having to create a completely separate scorecard.
body_text: Bringing new SDRs onto the team presents a common challenge for RevOps leaders: you want new hires contributing to team goals and participating in competitions from day one, but you also don't want to hold them to the same expectations as fully ramped reps. Fortunately, you don't need to create a separate scorecard just for ramping employees. Keep New Hires in the Same Role Group In most cases, Ambition recommends adding new SDRs to your existing scorecard role group rather than creating a dedicated "Ramping SDR" scorecard. This allows new hires to participate in the same dashboards, competitions, and reporting as the rest of the team while giving managers a consistent view of performance across the organization. The difference comes from the targets—not the scorecard itself. Use Custom Targets During Ramp Ambition allows you to set custom Activity and Objective Score targets for individual users while they ramp. For most organizations, a three-month ramp period is a good starting point, though you can make custom targets last as long as your onboarding program requires. Whether your ramp is 30 days, one quarter, or longer, targets can be updated at any time as reps progress toward full productivity. Once the rep is fully ramped, simply transition them to the standard targets used by the rest of the role group. Upload Targets Manually or in Bulk If you're onboarding a single rep, it's easy to add custom targets manually. Hiring a larger class? You can also upload custom targets via CSV, making it easy to assign multiple metrics for multiple users across weeks, months, or quarters in a single upload. This approach can save significant time for RevOps teams managing frequent onboarding cycles. Learn More For step-by-step instructions, check out these Help Center articles: How do I set custom targets or build ramp time into scorecards? What options do I have for uploading custom scorecard targets? Why would users in the same role have different targets on their scorecards? With custom targets, you can give new SDRs realistic goals while keeping them engaged with the rest of the team—a simple approach that scales much better than maintaining separate scorecards for every stage of ramp.

title: Trigger.dev v3: Durable Serverless functions. No timeouts.
summary: Write regular code and get durability with no timeouts. This means writing long-running tasks is far easier than before.
body_text: UPDATE: Trigger.dev v3 is now open access. Sign up for a free account . Trigger.dev v2 allows you to create durable long-running code that successfully avoids serverless timeouts. We achieve this by using a simple trick: caching completed chunks and replaying the function repeatedly until everything is finished. But there are some key downsides, some of which we can't fix while your code is executing inside your serverless functions. To solve this problem completely, and make it easy for you, we need to run your code and use a pretty amazing piece of technology: CRIU. More on that later. Durable long-running tasks Achieving long-running code isn't hard – you just need to have a long-running server and get the code onto it. Before "serverless" this was how everything worked. Localhost is a long-running server, and you can run code on it for as long as you want (or until your cat sits on the power button). There are a couple of issues though that need to be dealt with: Sometimes you want to wait for something to happen before continuing to the next line of code. That could be waiting until a specific point in time, for a specific event to happen, or for an HTTP request. Servers go down. Mostly this is caused by deploying new code. Servers do also (very rarely) fail. You don't want to start your task from scratch when this happens especially if mutations have happened that aren't idempotent . Writing regular async code with no timeouts and durability Our ultimate goal is to enable you to write normal async code, without timeouts and inherently durable, without resorting to awkward or error-prone syntax. This is how a task for purchasing movie theatre tickets will look in v3: trigger/ purchase.ts // Purchase flow for movie theatre tickets export const purchaseTicket = task({ id: "purchase-ticket", run: async ({ payload, }: { payload: { ticketId: string; userId: string }; }) => { // First we need to reserve the ticket const reservedTicket = await reserveTicket( payload.ticketId, payload.userId ); // Logs show up in the Trigger.dev UI console.log("Reserved ticket", { reservedTicket }); // Release the ticket if there are errors after this point rollback(async () => releaseTicket(reservedTicket.id)); // Give the user a 5 minute window to checkout. // Will throw an error if the user doesn't checkout in time const event = await events.waitForEvent({ event: "cart/checked-out", filter: { items: [payload.ticketId], userId: [payload.userId], }, timeout: { minutes: 5 }, }); console.log("Checked out", { checkout: event.payload }); // Now lookup the cart const cart = await db.findCart(event.payload.cartId); // and charge the user const charge = await stripe.charges.create({ amount: cart.total, currency: "usd", source: cart.paymentSource, description: `Ticket purchase for ${cart.items[0].name}`, }); console.log("Charged user", { charge }); // Refund the charge if there are any errors after this point rollback(async () => stripe.refunds.create({ charge: charge.id, }) ); // Finalize the ticket await finalizeTicket(reservedTicket.id, payload.userId); console.log("Finalized ticket"); //send confirmation email to the user const emailResult = await resend.emails.send({ from: " [email protected] ", to: cart.email, subject: "Ticket Purchase Confirmation", text: `Thanks for purchasing a ticket to ${cart.items[0].name}!`, }); if (emailResult.error || emailResult.data === null) { //this will cause the rollbacks to run throw new Error("Failed to send email"); } //send a Slack message to our team try { //this uses the official Slack SDK await slack.chat.postMessage({ channel: "C1234567890", text: `Someone just purchased a ticket to ${cart.items[0].name}!`, }); } catch (e) { // Don't throw an error here, since it's not critical console.error("Failed to send Slack notification", e); } }, }); Notice that many things from v2 are no longer needed. You don't need to use io.runTask to "cache" things for replays, and you can just use regular SDKs. In fact, you don't need to think about timeouts at all, since they don't exist. This is how you would trigger this purchase ticket task from your code: app/api/reserve/ route.ts import { purchaseTicket } from "~/trigger/purchase"; //you'd call this somewhere in your backend const taskHandle = await purchaseTicket.trigger({ payload: { ticketId: "tkt_12345", userId: "usr_12345", }, }); Note that this function returns a TaskHandle from the API, it does not wait until the task has completed. You can use the handle to look up the status of the task, cancel, retry and more. In the middle of the task there's this interesting piece of code: // Give the user a 5 minute window to checkout. // Will throw an error if the user doesn't checkout in time const event = await events.waitForEvent({ event: "cart/checked-out", filter: { items: [payload.ticketId], userId: [payload.userId], }, timeout: { minutes: 5 }, }); console.log("this will only be executed if a matching event is received"); When this code runs execution will pause and the server will get spun down. You could set a very long timeout here if you wanted, although it doesn't make sense for this example. You won't pay for compute time while it's waiting because the code is no longer executing. More on how this is achieved in a moment. For execution to continue you need to send a matching event when the user has actually pressed the checkout button: app/api/checkout/complete/ route.ts import { events } from "~/trigger/cart"; //somewhere in your backend code const sentEvent = await events.trigger({ event: "cart/checked-out", payload: { userId: "usr_12345", cartId: "cart_12345", }, }); How does this work? Checkpoints and Restoring When deployed, the code will run in a container that will be paused and resumed using Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace (CRIU) . CRIU is a Linux tool that allows you to freeze a running container and checkpoint it to disk. You can then restore the application from the checkpoint at a later time on a different machine. This is similar to how you can hibernate your computer and then resume it later. Google have been using this at scale internally since 2017 to pause low priority tasks and then continue them later on different machines. We will automatically checkpoint your task when: Function What it does wait.for() Waits for a specific period of time, e.g. 1 day. wait.until() Waits until the provided Date . wait.forRequest() Waits until a matching HTTP request is received, and gives you the data to continue with. event.waitForEvent() Waits for a matching event, like in the example above. task.triggerAndWait() Triggers a task and then waits until it's complete. You get the result data to continue with. task.batchTriggerAndWait() Triggers a task multiple times in parallel and then waits until they're all complete. You get the resulting data to continue with. In all of those situations the code will stop executing and will be resumed at a later date. You won't pay for compute time while it's waiting because the code is no longer executing. Where does this run? Your code will run in containers that support CRIU and workloads will scale up and down automatically. This is a major change from how it works in v2 where your code runs in your own serverless functions. This is required for zero-timeout durable code that is easy to write. It also has the benefit of simplifying costs. With v2 you pay us for orchestrating runs and you pay your cloud provider separately for compute time of your serverless functions. With v3 we provide durable compute and orchestration. We continue to be committed to open-source and self-hosting, more details on that later. No timeouts Most "serverless" platforms have timeouts. Some are very limiting like 10s on the Vercel free plan, others are higher like 15 minutes on AWS Lambda. Even 15 minutes is a problem for lots of tasks. Version 3 has no timeouts. You can run code for as long as you want and since execution can be paused it will be efficient. Versioning and immutable deploys Every deploy will create a new version of your tasks (e.g. 2024-01-19-1 ). When a run starts it is locked to that version and deployed versions aren't deleted or modified. This means that if you deploy a new version of your code after a task has started executing it will continue to run uninterrupted on the older version. This means: New deploys don't impact started tasks. You don't have to worry about breaking changes impacting running tasks. You can "migrate" running tasks to different versions, like re-running failed tasks on a new version of your code. Server hardware Most of the time you don't need beefy hardware or have unusual requirements. But sometimes you do. For example, you might be doing something CPU or RAM intense, or you might need to use FFmpeg or Puppeteer. You can specify machine specs on a task: trigger/ encode-video.ts export const encodeVideo = task({ id: "encodeVideo", machine: { image: "ffmpeg", cpu: 1, memory: 512, }, run: async ({ payload }: { payload: string }) => { //do stuff }, }); The DX for running locally and deploying Local development In your project you'll add your tasks inside trigger folders. We'll also have a trigger.config.js (or .mjs ) file with some settings. To run locally you'll use our new CLI dev command to run your tasks and simulate checkpointing. The behaviour will be the same as when deployed, except that it will run in a non-containerized Node.js process. Bundling and deployment There will be multiple ways to deploy: Use the CLI deploy command. Use GitHub Actions, or other CI/CD tools. A GitHub app on Trigger.dev. This will allow you to select a repo and we'll automatically deploy on every main and PR push. This is how Vercel works. Environment variables As we'll be running your code we will need Environment Variables for things like API keys. These will be securely stored in the same way we currently do for integration credentials. To save you having to add these in two places we will build integrations to sync them. First will probably be a Vercel integration that will sync overlapping secrets from Vercel to Trigger.dev. Integrations and webhooks In v2 integrations allow you to easily trigger jobs using webhooks and perform actions inside your run functions. For example, you can easily subscribe to new GitHub stars and send a Slack message with details about it . We support using API Keys and OAuth to authenticate with these services. Here's an example of a v3 task that sends Stripe subscription change notifications: trigger/ stripe.ts import { stripeWebhooks } from "@trigger.dev/sdk"; import { WebClient } from "@slack/web-api"; import { Resend } from "resend"; //this is similar to v2, but it is just for webhooks const stripe = stripeWebhooks({ id: "stripe", }); //these are the official Slack and Resend SDKS, NOT integrations const slack = new WebClient(process.env.SLACK_TOKEN!); const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY!); //this is how you'll subscribe to webhooks export const stripePlanChanged = stripe.task({ //the official webhook event names on: "customer.subscription.updated", id: "subscription-plan-changed", //payloads will be nicely typed as they are in v2 run: async ({ payload, context }) => { const user = await db.users.find({ stripeId: payload.customer }); const planId = getNewPlanId(payload); if (user.planId !== planId) { await db.users.update(user.id, { planId }); //this is using the official Resend SDK await resend.emails.send({ to: user.email, from: " [email protected] ", subject: "Your plan has changed", html: planEmail(payload), }); if (isPlanUpgraded(user.planId, planId)) { //this is using the official Slack SDK await slack.chat.postMessage({ text: `Plan upgraded for ${user.email} to ${planId}`, channel: "subscriptions", }); } } }, }); There are some important changes highlighted by this code: Webhooks work the same although the syntax is a bit nicer. Integrations aren't needed for performing actions inside run functions. As mentioned before, there is no need to wrap code in io.runTask to avoid timeouts. So you can just use SDKs like you normally would, use HTTP requests, or do anything that would normally work in a Node.js process. OAuth, credentials and Trigger.dev Connect In v2 we supported OAuth for integrations like Slack and Supabase. We will add support for OAuth in v3 that will work with webhooks and be available to use from our SDK. From the Trigger.dev app you can do an OAuth flow and we will securely store and refresh the tokens. From anywhere inside your code (including outside the trigger folder) you will be able to retrieve them using our SDK – so you can authenticate with APIs. Trigger.dev Connect will make it easy for you to collect OAuth and API keys from your users. You can then use them to subscribe to webhooks and use SDKs with your users' credentials. Open-source and self-hosting We continue to be 100% committed to open-source. We're figuring out how to make self-hosting v3 as easy as possible. It will be harder to self-host than v2 because it will no longer be possible to use a single Docker container and checkpointing will require CRIU-compatible system. CRIU is pretty widely supported across cloud providers. What about Trigger.dev v2? Trigger.dev v2 and v3 will live side-by-side. When creating a new project you will be able to choose which version you want to use. Feedback and the developer preview The continuous conversations and feedback we get from all of you has had a huge impact on how Trigger.dev works, and made us realize that we needed to make these changes. Please let us know your honest thoughts and concerns on Discord , Twitter , or via email .
